/Issued 101 PM MST Thu Nov 5 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

An approaching Pacific trough will displace the ridge aloft to 
the east and bring increased winds and even some spotty mostly 
mountain rain and snow showers later today. This system will 
generally be moisture starved and will offer little to no 
precipitation for most locations. H700 winds don’t look overly 
impressive, generally in the 30 to 40 kt range, but this will 
bring a definitive shift towards breezy to windy conditions, 
especially following the light wind regime of the last several 
days. 

Ridging aloft then builds back in for the first half of the 
weekend, but a trough passing to our north will tighten the 
pressure gradient along the Canadian border. Forecast soundings 
have been steadily becoming more bullish in regards to mountain 
wave activity bringing bouts of strong winds along the Northern 
Rocky Mountain Front and adjacent plains Friday into Saturday, 
with localized wind gusts between 60 and 80 mph. Winds don’t look 
quite as strong for the plains east of the highway 89 corridor, 
although gusts between 30 and 50 mph will be common. 

A slightly deeper trough moves in Sunday into Monday and brings 
another round of winds and some more light mountain precipitation,
mostly along the northern divide. This system will have a broader
wind shield with H700 peaking at well over 60 kts; however, there
may be more reliance on diurnal mixing for surface transfer 
momentum due to less ensemble confidence in more robust mountain 
waves. The winds certainly look to cover more real estate, but the
top winds may not be as strong as the previous system if mountain
waves are weaker and less frequent. The progressive westerly flow
pattern continues well into next week with another peak in winds 
heading towards the mid- week period. - RCG

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

High Winds from Friday afternoon through Saturday morning and Sunday…

Confidence in impactful winds occurring during the day on Sunday
has risen to the point where a High Wind Watch has been issued 
for the East Glacier Park Region, Northern and Southern High 
Plains, and Eastern Glacier/Western Toole/Central Pondera counties
from the late morning through early evening hours. BUFKIT 
analysis throughout this period indicates increasing, 
unidirectional cross barrier flow, which is likely to support 
momentum transfer to the surface solely through diurnal mixing 
processes. This alone supports the need for a High Wind Watch 
given the anomalous (2-3 standard deviations above normal) H700 
flow of 50-80kts moving over the region. Additionally within 
BUFKIT over this timeframe exists ideal thermal profiles to 
support mountain wave activity, which combined with a moderately 
strong surface pressure gradient will further enhance winds speeds
during the day on Sunday. 

For the timeframe from Friday afternoon through Saturday morning uncertainty
in high winds materializing still exists given a veering wind 
profile through the critical layer (i.e. ridgetop stability) from 
the surface. This veering profile during past events has limited 
how widespread the most intense winds are from the more 
traditional locations across the East Glacier Park Region, 
Northern and Southern High Plains, and Eastern Glacier/Western 
Toole/Central Pondera counties; however, some locations do still 
see impactful winds. For this reason the inherited High Wind Watch
was left as, but the Southern High Plains zone was added given 
the susceptibility of areas like Dellwo and Bynum hitting on 
criteria. If it was not’t for this veering profile BUFKIT 
soundings support another ideal thermal profile for mountain wave 
activity on Friday night, with a strong surface pressure gradient 
of 0.15 to 0.2 mb/km existing from the afternoon hours on Friday 
through Saturday morning along the immediate eastern slopes of the
Rocky Mountain Front.

The table below lists the reasonable low-end (25th Percentile), 
most likely (50th Percentile), and high-end (75th Percentile) 
wind gust scenarios within the NBM5.2 for select locations across 
the plains of Central and North Central Montana over the 
aforementioned timeframe. The low-end scenario has a 75% chance 
that wind gusts will exceed the listed value or a 25% chance that
gusts will be lower than what is listed while the high-end 
scenario has a 75% chance that wind gusts will be lower than what
is listed or a 25% chance that gusts will be higher than what is 
listed.
